briefing.opening: Good morning. We will now begin the climate briefing for September 13, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Deepening Climate Crisis: Compound Disasters and Public Health Threats
sections.content: News released today has once again underscored the widespread and severe impacts of climate change on humanity and ecosystems. The major floods in Nepal serve as a warning that compound disaster crises are becoming a reality [4], while instances of bears descending into residential areas in the U.S. in search of food illustrate ecosystem disruption due to climate change [2]. Health and medical alliances have classified climate change as a public health crisis [25, 27], with emergency room visits for heat-related illnesses actually increasing in the U.S. [26]. Furthermore, significant changes are being observed in agriculture and natural landscapes, such as difficulties in cultivating cauliflower in the UK due to climate change [39], and a bleak future for snow tourism being warned in Australia due to warm ski seasons [40]. Beyond these, climate change is exacerbating risks in the Adirondacks region [28], limiting insect survival capabilities [33], and even accelerating the excavation of Bronze Age archaeological sites [37], thereby causing crises in various sectors.

sections.title: 🌱 Accelerating Domestic Carbon Neutrality Policies and Renewable Energy Transition
sections.content: Amidst these crises, various efforts are continuing domestically to achieve carbon neutrality goals. KAIST and Lotte are accelerating the development of core technologies by establishing research hubs in carbon neutrality, bio-tech, and future food sectors [5, 6, 7, 12, 13]. Several local governments, including Buk-gu in Gwangju, Jeollanam-do, Seoul, Chungcheongnam-do, and Gyeongsangnam-do, have been selected as excellent examples of carbon neutrality, leading changes in local government policies [8, 11]. The Chungcheongnam-do Provincial Council has formed a special committee for a just transition towards carbon neutrality [9], and rural leaders in Yongin City received training pledging to practice carbon neutrality [10]. Corporations are also actively transitioning to renewable energy; an analysis suggests that telecom companies' net-zero achievement depends on renewable energy [14]. HD Hyundai Electric is procuring power through solar PV and PPAs, targeting RE100 by 2040 [18], and LS Electric has signed an MOU with Korea Midland Power for joint development of renewable energy projects [19]. Daejeon Dong-gu secured 1.22 billion KRW in national funding by achieving an 'A' grade in a renewable energy competition [16, 17]. Overall, positive movements for renewable energy expansion are observed across the country.

sections.title: 🌍 Expanding Horizons of International Cooperation and Climate Technology Innovation
sections.content: International cooperation and technological innovation efforts to address the climate crisis are also actively underway. South Korea and Malaysia reaffirmed the importance of international collaboration by discussing cooperation on climate change response [1], and Incheon City announced plans to apply Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to climate-vulnerable nations by hosting the World Climate Technology Forum [3]. Chairman Chey Tae-won emphasized energy security for both Korea and Japan, stating that solutions must be sought through diverse energy sources including renewable energy, hydrogen, and nuclear power [20]. Meanwhile, the UNFCCC at COP31 presented grid, ESS, methane, and waste management as key agendas in addition to increasing solar power generation, indicating that the scope of climate change response is further expanding [23].

sections.title: ⚠️ The AI Era: Surging Power Demand and New Challenges for Renewable Energy
sections.content: The recent advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology presents a new climate challenge: a surge in electricity demand. The explosive increase in power consumption by AI data centers has made the transition to renewable energy a critical variable for corporate survival [21, 24], re-emphasizing that renewable energy transition is the sole solution at the crossroads of climate justice [24]. Despite solar power generation capacity entering the 100 GW era [22], discussions are active regarding energy independence and the establishment of stable supply chains, including the need for a counterattack in the Korean solar supply chain [22]. Furthermore, policy and economic discussions related to renewable energy expansion are deepening, with proposals such as 'renewable energy regional dividends' in Australia, which would impose royalties on wind and solar power generation [15]. A wise response to these new challenges will be a crucial key to overcoming the climate crisis.

briefing.closing: Today's briefing has reaffirmed the severity of the climate crisis while highlighting various response efforts and new challenges both domestically and internationally. This is a critical juncture where sustained attention and action become even more important. This concludes today's climate briefing.
